To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the translocators YopB and/or YopD are secreted by Yersinia in amounts that are sufficient for translocation of Yop effectors.
the translocators YopB and/or YopD are not essential for Yop effector delivery into target HeLa cells and that LcrH dependent YopB and or YopD secretion is not required for this process.
the minimal secretion of translocators is sufficient for effector translocation, and that the LcrH dependent regulation of translocator secretion is very strict.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the Yersinia type III secretion system, with the aim to understand how the secretion of anti-host Yop effector proteins is controlled.
the regulation of Yersinia type III secretion, and the role of the YopB and D translocator proteins.
the molecular mechanisms by which the translocators are secreted by Yersinia, and the role of this secretion in the translocation of effector Yop proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Y. pseudotuberculosis and Y. pestis are able to translocate Yop effector proteins into target cells in the absence of a detectable YopD- and YopB-dependent pore.
the YopB/YopD translocator system is not regulated by LcrH.
Yersinia translocates Yops in a highly regulated manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the translocator proteins YopB and/or YopD can be secreted in minimal amounts to allow for effector translocation.
LcrH mutants are not good models for studying Yersinia translocation.
Yersinia has evolved a sophisticated regulatory mechanism to ensure that the translocator proteins are only secreted at levels required to deliver the effectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
YopB- or YopD-dependent pore formation may be a secondary consequence of translocon formation and that YopB and/or YopD secretion may not be the limiting factor in Yop effector translocation.
Y. pseudotuberculosis and Y. enterocolitica are remarkably efficient in translocating effectors into eukaryotic host cells.
the Yersinia type III secretion system can deliver effectors into eukaryotic host cells without forming detectable translocator pores.
